name: Alveolar macrophage
blurb: A human alveolar macrophage: a large, rounded scavenger cell that lives in the air space of the lung, ruffled and reaching out fingers of membrane to engulf dust and microbes.
note: Model: a human alveolar macrophage, cut through its middle. Measured in human lung: its diameter (21 µm, cells washed out of the lung) and volume (about 5,000 µm³), and the width of its nucleus (8.3 µm, lung sections). Illustrative: the number, length and place of the pseudopods, the ruffling, the shape and place of the nucleus, the number and size of the mitochondria, lysosomes and engulfed dust particles and surfactant sacs, and the colours.

diameter.note: 21.2 ± 0.3 µm (mean ± the reported ±, 10 healthy non-smoking volunteers); cells washed out of the lung and measured in suspension, where they are round. Clinging to the wall they spread flatter. Range shown is the reported mean ± 0.3 µm only; the spread among individuals is not in the source.

volume.calc: measured volume 4990 ± 174 µm³ by electrical-resistance flow cytometry; a sphere 21.2 µm across has 4/3 x pi x 10.6³ = 4,989 µm³, so the drawn ball matches it before the pseudopods are added
volume.note: same 10 volunteers; range is the reported mean ± 174 µm³ only, not the spread among individuals

nucleus_diameter.note: 8.33 ± 0.86 µm (SD), lung macrophages in sections of 8 normal human lungs; nuclei measured in sections may read a little small

nucleus_share.calc: a sphere 8.33 µm across (303 µm³) over the cell volume 4,990 µm³; the two numbers come from different studies and the nucleus is not truly round, so this is approximate

pseudopod_length.note: illustrative: pseudopods change within minutes as the cell moves and feeds

share_in_air_spaces.note: abstract: 95% of alveolar macrophages in gas-exchange air spaces, 5% in airways; Results text: over 97%; right upper lobes only, 12 donors without lung disease (6 smokers, 6 nonsmokers); both free and wall-attached cells seen; the paper gives no free versus attached percentages

size_um.note: illustrative: the width of 8.3 µm is measured (crapo1982) but the oval shape, the other two axes and the position of the nucleus are not

count.note: illustrative: a cell that digests what it engulfs holds many

not_drawn: the layer of surfactant the cell sits in

cut: The cell is cut through its middle: a ruffled outline with finger-like pseudopods, an oval nucleus with a nucleolus near the centre (position illustrative), mitochondria and many small lysosomes through the cytoplasm, and a few larger bags near the edge holding engulfed particles.

colours.convention: Cell membrane pale pink, the inside dark; nucleus violet; mitochondria orange; lysosomes green; engulfed particles grey-brown. All are a code, not the real colours.

cytosol.name: Cytosol
cytosol.about: The watery inside of the cell, crowded with proteins.

phagosome.name: Phagosome with dust
phagosome.about: A sac of membrane round particles the cell has swallowed from the air in the lung: dust, soot or microbes. In a smoker or a city dweller these dark particles build up in the cells. The number and size drawn are illustrative.

surfactant_inclusion.name: Swallowed surfactant
surfactant_inclusion.about: Pale sacs of surfactant, the film of lipids and proteins that lines the air spaces. Alveolar macrophages take it up and break it down, helping to keep the amount right. Their number here is illustrative.

about: The ball is 21.2 µm across, the size measured for human alveolar macrophages washed out of the lung; its volume is {drawn.cellVolume} µm³ with the pseudopods, against 4,990 µm³ measured. This is large for a body cell and about four times the volume of the same cell in a rat (1,166 µm³) or hamster (1,328 µm³) in the same study.

The cell lives in the air space of the lung, not inside the wall: most of these cells (about 95% in one count of human lungs) sit in the gas-exchange air spaces, some free and some attached to the wall. Clinging to the wall it flattens, so this round shape is the one seen in suspension.

When it meets a particle or microbe it wraps a pseudopod or a thin ruffled sheet round it and pinches it off into a bag, a phagosome, which then fuses with lysosomes full of digestive enzymes. {drawn.phagosomes} phagosomes are drawn holding dark dust, with {drawn.surfactantInclusions} pale sacs of swallowed surfactant, the lipid film that lines the air spaces. Their number, place and size are illustrative.

{drawn.nuclei} nucleus and {drawn.mitochondria} of about {drawn.mitochondriaWanted} mitochondria are drawn. The nucleus width is measured; its oval shape and position, and every organelle count, are illustrative. The rough endoplasmic reticulum, the ribosomes and the filament skeleton are not drawn.
